analysis.one_liner: Extends bank community-reinvestment lending and disclosure rules to securities firms, mortgage lenders, and insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 29 House sponsors in July 2000, it sat in two committees and two subcommittees until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended the Community Reinvestment Act — the 1977 law requiring banks to serve low- and moderate-income neighborhoods — to parts of the financial industry banks had just been allowed to merge with under the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley law. Securities firms, mortgage banks, and insurance companies would have faced their own community-service ratings, and insurers would have had to report by census tract where they sell, deny, and cancel policies. It died in House subcommittees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income borrowers, homebuyers, and neighborhoods — especially minority communities — that banks, mortgage lenders, securities firms, and insurers currently do not have to serve. The bill's stated findings note the homeownership gap (46.9% for Black families and 46.2% for Hispanic families versus 66.7% overall) and a minority median net worth of $16,400 versus $94,900 for white families [S3]. Small businesses, farms, and minority- and women-owned firms would gain from expanded lending data disclosure, and consumers would gain from public data on where insurers deny and cancel coverage [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Underserved borrowers, minority homebuyers, small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Would have subjected nonbank affiliates of bank holding companies — the securities, insurance, and mortgage businesses banks newly acquired under Gramm-Leach-Bliley — to the same Community Reinvestment Act obligations as banks, closing the loophole that let lending activity move outside the law's reach [S2, S3].

Would have imposed affirmative community-service obligations on securities companies, mortgage banks, and insurance companies, each rated on how well it serves low- and moderate-income neighborhoods in its assessment areas, with poor performers facing restrictions — including a ban on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buying their mortgages [S2, S3].
Would have lowered a financial institution's rating if regulators found predatory lending or discriminatory practices, making redlining and predatory loan terms a direct business cost [S2, S3].

Would have created an Insurance Disclosure Act requiring insurers to report, by census tract, where policies are issued, denied, cancelled, or non-renewed, and the race and gender of policyholders — HMDA-style sunlight on insurance redlining — with civil penalties up to $5,000 per day for violations [S2, S3].

Would have required banks to collect race, gender, revenue, and census-tract data on small business and farm loan applicants, and barred regulators from exempting big institutions from that reporting, making discriminatory business lending visible [S2, S3].

Would have required public notice, comment, and public meetings before large bank holding company mergers and financial holding company formations, with regulators weighing risks to depositors, the financial system, and community reinvestment records [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and bank holding companies, securities firms, mortgage banks, insurance companies, and private mortgage insurers, who would bear compliance and data-reporting costs, community-service ratings, and potential restrictions on their activities or their loans' eligibility for purchase by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac [S2, S3]. Some of those costs could be passed on to customers through fees or reduced service in marginal markets [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, insurers, mortgage and securities firms

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden falls heavily on insurers, insurance agents, and smaller financial institutions; the bill itself directs regulators to minimize paperwork burdens on independent agents and small insurers, an acknowledgment that compliance costs are real and fall on small businesses as well as large firms [S3].

The enforcement design is sweeping: it hands HUD power over insurance — traditionally regulated by the states — and lets the Secretary bar Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from buying loans from noncompliant mortgage banks and insurers, a lever that could reduce mortgage availability in some markets if misapplied [S2, S3].

Collecting race, gender, and census-tract data on insurance policyholders raises privacy questions for consumers; the bill tries to manage this by making disclosure voluntary for applicants and shielding individual insurers' loss experience from public release [S3].

Community-service obligations and ratings could lead some firms to avoid serving certain assessment areas altogether rather than risk a poor rating, a well-known design tension in CRA-style regimes that the bill addresses only through rating mechanics, not guarantees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — bringing the roughly 40% of financial-industry assets that had moved outside the CRA's reach back under community reinvestment obligations, and shining the same data light on insurance that already existed for mortgages — is large and aimed at a documented racial and income gap in homeownership and wealth [S3]. The costs are compliance and reporting burdens concentrated on the financial industry, plus a genuinely heavy-handed enforcement structure centered on HUD [S3]. An honest supporter would concede the enforcement design could have been leaner; an honest opponent would have to concede the bill targets real, measurable disparities. The bill never received committee scrutiny, so its practical flaws were never tested or fixed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees in each, no committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Barrett introduced the bill on July 19, 2000 with 29 original sponsors, all Democrats except independent Rep. Bernie Sanders, explicitly to make community reinvestment 'keep pace' with bank-securities-insurance mergers allowed by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act enacted the year before [S1, S3, S5].
The Speaker referred it to both the Banking and Financial Services Committee and the Commerce Committee, a dual referral that requires two committees to act [S5].
In August 2000 it was sent to subcommittees — Finance and Hazardous Materials in Commerce, and Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit in Banking — the standard place bills go to wait [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the last action of any kind was the subcommittee referral on August 16, 2000, four and a half months before the Congress ended [S5].
Because the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, the bill died and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, securities firms, mortgage lenders, and insurance companies came out ahead: they kept the expanded freedoms of Gramm-Leach-Bliley without any of the community-reinvestment, anti-predatory-lending, or disclosure obligations this bill would have attached to them. Low- and moderate-income and minority communities lost the chance at expanded access to credit, mortgages, and insurance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that avoided new obligations

for.name: Rep. Thomas M. Barrett
for.role: Sponsor, House Banking and Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day it was introduced.

for.name: 28 of 211 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including senior financial-services members such as Barney Frank and John LaFalce's committee colleagues, plus Congressional Black and Hispanic Caucus members.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the only non-Democrat among the 29 sponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jim Leach
against.role: Chair, House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the primary committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in the Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee from August 16, 2000 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the second committee of referral, never acted; the bill's insurance provisions sat in the Finance and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee from August 8, 2000 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Financial services industry (banking, insurance, securities, mortgage lending)
against.role: Industries that would have been regulated
against.what_they_did: Firms that had just won expanded merger freedoms under the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act broadly opposed extending CRA-style obligations to insurance companies, securities firms, and nonbank mortgage lenders.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone independent; no Republican cosponsored, and with Republican chairs controlling both committees of referral the bill never reached the floor, so no roll-call vote ever recorded where the parties stood.

industries.note: Would have faced a first-ever federal affirmative obligation to serve low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, plus census-tract disclosure of policy denials, cancellations, and agent terminations by race, enforced by HUD with daily civil penalties. Insurers currently face none of this, and the bill's own findings cite research tying minority zip codes to more state-backed last-resort insurance, evidence the private market already avoids these neighborhoods [S3].

Would have been brought under community-reinvestment ratings for the first time, with predatory lending lowering their scores and persistent failure letting HUD bar Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from buying their loans — their main funding channel [S2, S3].

Would have been rated by the SEC on serving low- and moderate-income customers and making community development investments, with low minimum account balances and fee structures counting toward their score — obligations that did not exist before or after [S2, S3].

Would have lost the ability to route lending through nonbank affiliates outside the CRA, faced neighborhood-by-neighborhood ratings, rating penalties for predatory lending, and public notice-and-comment before major mergers — reversing part of the deregulatory sweep of Gramm-Leach-Bliley [S2, S3].
Would have had to make HMDA-equivalent data public about whose loans they insure, with HUD empowered to compel reporting if they did not voluntarily comply [S2, S3].
